opus-5.5.text:
I think the useful way to frame it is to separate *what* to do from *how* to do it.

Human video is incredibly rich in the "what" layer. When you watch someone cook or tidy a room, you see the task structure: which objects matter, what order things happen in, where the hand goes, what the goal state looks like, how objects move once they're manipulated. That's high-level intent, object-centric motion, and a lot of common sense about how the world responds to actions. Robots can learn much of that from human video because it's largely independent of whose body is doing the work. A mug ends up in the dishwasher whether a human hand or a robot gripper put it there.

The "how" layer is much harder to transfer. That's the low-level control: the exact forces, the contact dynamics, the fine finger coordination, the compliance. A human hand has over twenty degrees of freedom, tactile sensing everywhere, and a lifetime of motor learning. A robot might have a parallel-jaw gripper and a wrist camera. So the embodiment gap really bites at the level of joint torques and contact-rich interaction. You can't just copy the motor commands, because there aren't any to copy. You only see the outcome visually, and the robot's body is different.

So in practice, my group and others in the field have converged on a kind of hierarchical view. Use human data, which is cheap and abundant and can be collected in the wild, to learn the parts that are embodiment-agnostic: task planning, where to attend, hand or object trajectories in 3D space, affordances. Then use a smaller amount of robot data, from teleoperation or the robot's own experience, to ground those plans in the robot's actual body and close the loop on the physical details.

The interesting research question is where exactly to draw that line, and it keeps moving. As we get better at representing actions in a shared space, for example tracking hand poses and mapping them to robot end-effector motions, or collecting human data with wearable devices that capture more of the 3D and egocentric structure, more of the "how" becomes learnable from humans too. My view is that human data won't replace robot data entirely, but it can carry most of the weight, and robot data becomes the alignment signal rather than the main source of knowledge. That's how we get to the scale needed for generalist robots without teleoperating millions of hours.

r001.rationale: It says a mug reaches the dishwasher whether a human hand or robot gripper puts it there, expressing that the outcome is independent of who causes it when the robot can produce it.

r002.rationale: It says better action representations and hand-to-end-effector mapping could make more of the “how” learnable from human data, but does not state that this depends on the robot having manipulation capabilities sufficiently similar to a human's.

r003.rationale: It states that exact forces and contact control are difficult to transfer and that motor commands cannot be copied because they are not visible in human video.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question we think about constantly, because human video is this enormous, almost free source of data, but it's also deeply misleading if you're not careful about what you take from it.

The way I think about it is to split "acting on the world" into layers. At the top you have intent and task structure: what are the subgoals, in what order do things happen, what does the world look like before and after a step. Human video is fantastic for that. If I watch a thousand people make coffee, I learn that you open the lid, you add grounds, you add water, you close it, and I learn what a "done" state looks like. None of that depends on having a human hand. That's a representation of the world and of tasks, and it transfers pretty cleanly.

The middle layer is something like affordances and interaction structure. Where do you grasp a cabinet handle, which direction does a drawer move, what parts of the scene are relevant. Human video still gives you a lot here, because the physics of the object are the same whether a person or a robot is touching it. You have to be a bit more careful, because the human hand is doing things a parallel-jaw gripper can't, but the geometry of the object and the rough contact regions carry over.

The bottom layer is the actual motor control: the forces, the finger coordination, the millisecond-level feedback when something slips. That is where human video mostly fails you. First, the embodiment is different, so the exact trajectory is wrong for the robot. Second, and this is the bigger issue, video doesn't contain the information you'd need anyway. You can't see force, you can't see tactile feedback, you often can't even see the contact because the hand occludes it. So trying to copy that layer from video is a bit like trying to learn to play piano by watching a silent film.

So in practice the recipe we've converged on is: use human video to learn the high-level stuff, the task plans, the visual representations, the "what should happen next" predictions, and then use a much smaller amount of robot data, or interaction in simulation, to ground that into real low-level control. The video tells the robot what to do and roughly where to put its hand. The robot's own experience tells it how.

The honest caveat is that the boundary between those layers isn't fixed. As we get better at inferring 3D hand pose and contact from video, some of what I just called "low-level" starts to become learnable from human data too. But the principle holds: the more something depends on the specific body doing it, the less you should expect to read it off a video of a different body.

r001.rationale: The response says object physics are the same whether a person or robot is touching it, and that world states and task structure transfer. This conveys that world changes carry over when the robot can perform the relevant interaction.

r002.rationale: It says human video can reveal affordances and rough contact regions, but does not state that transfer depends on the robot having manipulation capabilities sufficiently similar to a human's.

r003.rationale: It says human video mostly fails to teach the motor-control layer, including forces and finger coordination, because video lacks force and tactile information and the embodiment differs.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate two things: understanding what to do and understanding how to physically do it. Human video gives you a lot of information about the first part—what objects matter, how a task breaks down into steps, and what changes in the world when someone succeeds. If you watch someone make coffee, you can learn that they pick up a cup, put it under the machine, and press a button.

But video doesn’t directly tell you the forces involved, how firmly to grasp the cup, or what to do when it starts slipping. And a human hand is different from a robot gripper, so you can’t simply copy the motion. The robot needs experience with its own body to learn those details.

So the distinction I would make is between learning the structure and goals of an interaction from human video, and grounding that knowledge in actions the robot can reliably execute. They’re connected, but observing an action and being able to perform it are different capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says video reveals what changes when a task succeeds, but does not say those changes are independent of whether a human or robot causes them, provided the robot can produce them.

r002.rationale: It says a human hand differs from a robot gripper and the robot needs experience with its own body. It does not state that sufficiently similar manipulation capabilities let video teach how the robot embodiment affects the world.

r003.rationale: The response says video does not directly reveal physical execution details such as forces and grip, and that the robot needs its own experience to learn them. This communicates that the control needed to execute actions cannot be learned directly from human video.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate what to do from how to do it. Human video can show a robot what a task looks like: which objects matter, how the steps fit together, and what a successful outcome is. If you watch someone make coffee, for example, you can learn a lot about the sequence without knowing the forces they're applying.

The harder part is learning the physical interaction. How tightly should you grasp the cup? How much force do you need to open a drawer? Those things aren't always visible, and a robot's body is different from a person's. So human video can provide useful structure and guidance, but the robot still needs experience acting in the world to connect that understanding to its own movements and the feedback it gets.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes task structure from physical interaction, but does not state that the world’s changes are independent of whether a human or robot causes them, provided the robot can produce them.

r002.rationale: It says human video offers useful structure and guidance, but does not say video can teach world effects when the robot’s manipulation capabilities are sufficiently similar to a human’s.

r003.rationale: It says physical interaction and forces are hard to infer and that the robot needs experience, but does not specifically state that the joint-level control required to execute an action cannot be learned directly from human video.
